content: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) refers to an infection that affects the female reproductive organs, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries. As the infection progresses, it can lead to the formation of scar tissue and adhesions that involve nearby tissues and organs. This process may result in tissue necrosis, with or without the formation of abscesses. In some cases, pus may be released into the peritoneal cavity. Notably, two-thirds of patients with laparoscopic evidence of prior PID were unaware that they had ever experienced the condition. PID is frequently associated with sexually transmitted infections (STIs), as it is a common consequence of such infections. However, the term PID is broad and can encompass infections caused by viruses, fungi, or parasites, though bacterial infections are the most common cause. PID should be classified based on the affected organs, the stage of the infection, and the causative organism(s). While STIs are a common cause, other routes of infection include lymphatic spread, postpartum or post-abortal infections (following miscarriage or abortion), intrauterine device (IUD)-related infections, and hematogenous spread. PID occurs when bacteria ascend from the vagina or cervix into the upper reproductive organs. While many organisms can cause PID, the majority of cases are linked to gonorrhea and chlamydia, two prevalent bacterial STIs. Certain factors increase the risk of developing PID. These include a history of PID, recent sexual activity, the onset of menstruation, the presence of an IUD, or having a sexual partner with an STI. Acute PID is unlikely in the absence of recent sexual intercourse or IUD use. Although PID itself can be treated and cured, the damage caused by the infection may be permanent. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to prevent long-term damage to the reproductive system. Prevention is also essential to preserve reproductive health. If the infection is confined to the lower reproductive tract, successful treatment is less likely to result in reproductive complications. However, infections involving the fallopian tubes or ovaries are more likely to lead to serious complications. Diagnosing PID can be challenging because its symptoms are often subtle or mild. Many cases go undetected because patients or healthcare providers fail to recognize the significance of nonspecific symptoms. There are no definitive tests for PID, so diagnosis is typically based on clinical findings. Some patients may not exhibit any symptoms, while others may experience fever, cervical motion tenderness, lower abdominal pain, unusual vaginal discharge, painful intercourse, or irregular menstrual bleeding. It is important to note that PID can cause significant harm even in the absence of noticeable symptoms. Additional signs and symptoms may include foul-smelling vaginal discharge, painful urination, and, in rare cases, pain in the right upper abdomen. No single laboratory test is sufficiently sensitive or specific to diagnose PID. Laboratory findings that indicate infection include elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and white blood cell (WBC) count. A sensitive serum pregnancy test should be performed to rule out ectopic pregnancy. Gram staining and smears are useful for identifying rare or more serious organisms. Pelvic ultrasound is a valuable diagnostic tool for PID. It can help visualize the pelvic area to determine if the fallopian tubes are enlarged or if an abscess is present. Pelvic and vaginal ultrasounds are also helpful in differentiating PID from ectopic pregnancy, particularly in pregnancies over six weeks. Other diagnostic studies, such as culdocentesis, can help distinguish hemoperitoneum (caused by ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemorrhagic cyst) from pelvic sepsis (caused by salpingitis, ruptured pelvic abscess, or ruptured appendix). Treatment for PID typically involves antibiotic therapy, which is tailored to the causative organism. If the patient does not show improvement within two to three days of starting antibiotics, they should return to the hospital for further evaluation and treatment. Antibiotics may be administered orally and/or intravenously to ensure prompt and effective treatment. Hospitalization may be necessary in cases of tubo-ovarian abscess, severe illness, immunodeficiency, pregnancy, cervical incompetence, or when life-threatening conditions cannot be ruled out. Treating sexual partners for STIs is a crucial component of managing and preventing PID. Partners of patients diagnosed with PID within the past six months should also be treated to prevent reinfection. Psychotherapy is recommended for women diagnosed with PID, as they may experience anxiety about the possibility of recurrence. Patients are encouraged to communicate any concerns or uncertainties with their healthcare provider, particularly a specialist such as a gynecologist, and to seek follow-up care. In cases where symptoms persist or an abscess does not resolve, surgery may be required. Complications of PID, such as chronic pelvic pain and scarring, can be challenging to manage, though they may improve with surgical intervention.
